opus-5.5.text:
Evaluation is honestly one of the things we obsess over most, because in this field it's very easy to fool yourself. With language models you can look at an output and get a pretty good gut sense of whether it's good. With a predicted protein structure or a designed binder, you can't eyeball it. A structure can look beautiful and be completely wrong in the ways that matter, like the exact geometry of an interface or how a small molecule sits in a pocket. So we've had to be really disciplined about measurement.

A few principles guide us. The first is being rigorous about data leakage. Biology has a lot of near-duplicates. The same protein family shows up again and again, and if you're not careful about how you split train and test, often by time cutoffs and by sequence or structural similarity, you end up measuring memorization rather than generalization. We spend a lot of effort making sure our benchmarks reflect the setting people actually care about, which is new targets and new chemistry the model hasn't seen.

The second is making sure the metrics track real-world usefulness. Aggregate structure-accuracy numbers are useful, but what a drug discovery scientist cares about is narrower: did you get the binding mode right, is your confidence calibrated so I know when to trust you, will this design actually bind when we make it in the lab. So we break evaluation down by the tasks that matter, like antibody-antigen interfaces, protein-ligand complexes, and harder targets, rather than hiding behind one average.

The third, and probably the most important for staying at the frontier, is closing the loop with the wet lab. Computational benchmarks are necessary but not sufficient. Eventually you have to synthesize molecules, test them, and see what the hit rates really are. That's the ground truth, and it keeps us honest. When we started seeing meaningful success rates on design tasks that historically needed huge screening campaigns, that told us much more than any in-silico number could.

Last, evals shape what we build. When we look at where models fail, whether that's particular target classes, conformational flexibility, or overconfidence in certain regimes, that tells us where to focus next. A good eval suite is really a map of what you don't yet understand. If your benchmarks are saturated, you're not measuring the frontier anymore, so we're always building harder ones.

r001.rationale: The response says evaluation failures show where to focus next and that evals shape what Chai builds, conveying evaluation as a guide for iterative model improvement.

r002.rationale: It mentions meaningful success rates on tasks that historically required large screening campaigns, but does not state that Chai 2 achieved a rate making large library screening unnecessary.

r003.rationale: The response describes using wet-lab results and failures to guide future work, but does not describe reinforcing emerging model capabilities until they are production-ready.

fable-5.1.text:
Evaluation is honestly the thing I think about most, because in our field it's the whole game. If you're training a language model, you've got an enormous stream of text and benchmarks that roughly track what you care about. For us, the thing we actually care about is harder and slower to measure, and often noisy. So the real question is how you build a signal that's tight enough and fast enough that you can iterate on the model like a normal machine learning team would.

The way we think about it internally is in tiers. The first is the in-silico stuff, the standard public benchmarks everyone compares against. Those are useful for sanity checking and for seeing where you stand relative to the field, but they saturate quickly, and they're also where you can fool yourself the most. A model can look great on a held-out benchmark and still not have learned the thing you actually want, because the test is "reproduce what already exists," not "produce something genuinely new that holds up."

The second tier is our own designed evaluations. We build sets specifically around the failure modes we care about, especially novelty and generalization. We want to know whether the model is reasoning or just memorizing, so we construct tests where memorization doesn't help.

And the third tier is the real-world feedback loop, the slow experimental signal that grounds everything. That's the ground truth, and the whole point of the first two tiers is to let us place fewer, smarter bets there. When those three line up, we know the model is really moving, and when they diverge, that disagreement is usually where the most interesting learning is.

r001.rationale: The response says evaluations should provide a signal fast and precise enough to iterate on the model, and that the first two tiers guide smarter experimental bets.

r002.rationale: It does not mention Chai 2, a success rate, or avoiding large library screening.

r003.rationale: It discusses evaluation tiers and model progress, but not reinforcing emerging capabilities until they are production-ready.

astra-6.text:
The key is making sure our evaluations measure the thing we actually care about: whether we can design molecules that work in the lab. A model can look better on a computational benchmark without becoming more useful for drug discovery.

So you need that feedback loop between modeling and experiments. You make predictions, test them, and use the results to understand where the model succeeds and where it breaks down. Those failures help you decide what data you need and what to change in the next model.

And as the models improve, the evaluations have to get harder. You want to test generalization to new targets and new design problems, rather than keep optimizing against a benchmark you already do well on. That’s what makes evaluation a guide for research, rather than just a score you report.

sol-6.1.text:
We try to make evaluation a tight loop between the models we build and what actually works in the lab. A model can look better on a computational benchmark, but the question is whether that improvement translates into molecules with the properties we care about.

So we use computational evaluations to iterate quickly, and experimental results to check whether we’re measuring the right things. When those disagree, that’s especially useful: it tells us where our benchmarks or our models are missing something.

The goal is to make evaluation a tool for deciding what to build next. Where does the model fail? Which failures matter most? And what experiment would help us distinguish between competing ideas? That feedback loop is what keeps the research moving forward.

r001.rationale: It presents evaluation as a feedback loop for iterating on models and deciding what to build next.
